newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU covert deals suggest members are already known.
newsitem.headline: EMU covert deals suggest members are already known.

text.p: Speculation of a covert deal to keep Italy out of monetary union falsely suggests that leading European Union countries already know who will qualify for the single currency next year, EU officials say.

Talk of a deal to exclude questionable economies from the first wave of European economic and monetary union (EMU) resurfaced on Wednesday when an Italian newspaper said Germany and France were negotiating to bar Italy and Spain.

The report produced a chorus of denials from Bonn, Paris and Rome, and once again raised the uncomfortable question over the willingness of core European countries like Germany to accept broad membership in the euro.
While EU monetary officials deny the existence of any "plan," thinking along the lines described in the news report is likely being carried out in certain European capitals.
"I think the idea is sort of gaining ground here and there," said one senior EU official.
"But there should be one thing that is absolutely clear: for latecomers no exceptions are made. For them sustainability is the key word."
In a separate report on Thursday, the same newspaper, Il Sole 24 Ore, said Paris and Bonn will try to reach a consensus by September this year on which EU countries will be able to qualify for EMU.

But just how such a deal would work in practice nobody quite knows. Moreover, the idea such a strategy exists presumes that countries like Italy or Spain would meet the convergence criteria of the Maastricht treaty.
If they did not qualify there would be no need for a secret plan, officials say.
"What is least clear is on what kind of assumption regarding the out-turn for 1997 and 1998 budget deficits these plans are based," added another official.
Analysts note that the fiscal outlook for Italy has in fact worsened in light of its latest mini-budget, widely criticised for containing too many one-off saving measures.

The issue of "sustainable convergence," a key element of the Maastricht Treaty and one that is being mentioned more and more by EU officials, means the EU will look ahead to 1998 budgets in determining which countries qualify.

For governments currently struggling to meet the deficit and debt criteria this might be a good thing as they can argue that a glance into 1998 would show they could indeed bring their finances under control.
But for those whose 1997 budgets contain a significant number of temporary saving measures, 1998 could prove fatal to the chances for EMU entry in 1999.

Analysts say the real issue behind the speculation of covert plots and deals is the credibility of the euro, and in this regard there may be legitimate concern that a currency launched with too many members would be perceived as weak.
"I think Germany wants Italy out of the first wave no matter what their record on convergence is," said one economist at a large investment bank in London.
Many in the past have noted that Maastricht's convergence criteria were designed with the belief that southern European countries like Italy would never be able to meet them on schedule.
The surprise is that such countries have made remarkable progress in whipping their economies and budgets into shape and are in fact coming very close to the criteria.

The one southern country that appears best placed is Portugal, and some believe its timely inclusion in the euro would serve two important purposes: It would first dispel the notion that there is a conspiracy by Germany and France against southern European members and it would also allow for a credible start to EMU.
Given Portugal's small size, its influence on the initial euro area would be negligible, say officials.
